entry.title: JACOBS -v- HER HONOUR MAGISTRATE WARD [2026] WASC 435
entry.content:
Ms Jacobs, a public housing tenant, sought judicial review of a Magistrates Court decision dismissing her Residential Tenancies Act claims and finding no jurisdiction over her Australian Consumer Law claims. The Supreme Court found a reasonably arguable case and identified jurisdictional errors arising from denial of natural justice and misconstruction of RTA provisions. The decision was quashed in part and remitted to the Magistrates Court, differently constituted.

Key holding: On judicial review under s 36 MCA and s 26(2) RTA, an inferior court’s decision is affected by jurisdictional error only where it fails to exercise judicial power itself, including by misconceiving its statutory function or power, rather than merely making an error within jurisdiction.

These cases confirm that the relevant inquiry upon an application for judicial review of a decision of an inferior court is whether there has been a failure of the judicial officer to exercise judicial power itself or whether the judicial officer has merely made an error while exercising that judicial power. The former will generally constitute jurisdictional error; the latter will not.

Supreme Court of Western Australia, 9 Oct 2026, [2026] WASC 435

entry.title: Simin Gharibian v Propix Pty Ltd, trading as Jamberoo Recreational Park [2007] NSWCA 151
entry.content:
The appellant suffered serious injuries on a toboggan ride at Jamberoo Recreational Park when sudden rain caused the brakes to fail and the toboggan crashed into an airbag. The NSW Court of Appeal held that the respondent breached the implied warranty under s 74 of the Trade Practices Act, and by majority made orders in favour of the appellant on liability only, remitting damages to the District Court.

entry.title: Mr Marcus Watzlaff v Secure Parking Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 1408
entry.content:
Mr Watzlaff was employed as a Compliance Manager by Secure Parking following a Federal Court order requiring a compliance officer. His role was made redundant and he was dismissed after consultation. The Commission found the dismissal was harsh, unjust and unreasonable, rejecting the genuine redundancy defence, and ordered reinstatement (provisionally to a part-time Compliance Manager role on pro rata terms), finding no loss of trust and confidence preventing reinstatement.

entry.title: Frank Kalayzich v Australian Football League [2025] FWC 2492
entry.content:
Mr Frank Kalayzich, an AFL umpires coach with 40 years of service, was dismissed after a physical altercation and aggressive conduct towards a member of the public at North Sydney Oval. He applied for an unfair dismissal remedy seeking reinstatement, alleging the dismissal was procedurally and substantively unfair. The Commission found the AFL had a valid reason for dismissal, procedural fairness was afforded, and although his long service carried weight, his limited remorse meant the dismissal was not harsh, unjust or unreasonable.

Fair Work Commission, 25 Nov 2025, [2025] FWC 2492
